samples.summary: Image gate hard-requires local DNS resolution, breaking exports on proxy-only / DNS-restricted machines — including images served by the configured API server
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` unconditionally calls `await resolveHost(url, lookup, target)` (line 394) for every non-literal host, and `resolveHost` converts any lookup failure or empty answer into `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR')` (lines 267-279). This runs *before* `planHop`, so it runs even when `proxyForUrl()` would have routed the request through an egress proxy that resolves names itself — exactly the machines the new proxy support was added for. It also runs when the verdict is already decided: for the ordinary case `sameName === true` (image hosted at the server's own hostname) every address is allowed by the filter regardless, yet the lookup is still awaited and can fail the whole export. Previously `docs export` / `slides export` only needed the proxy/transport to resolve the name, never the local resolver.

samples.summary: `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` refusal can break the ordinary browser sign-in when the frontend origin is cross-site from `VITE_BACKEND_API_URL`, or when the login link is reached through a cross-site redirect chain
samples.evidence: `assertBrowserInitiated` throws `BadRequestException` for any value outside `{none, same-origin, same-site}` (lines 145-154), and it runs for the *browser* flow too (`canActivate` line 95, applied to `GET /auth/github` at auth.controller.ts:91). The frontend's sign-in link is `packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:63` → `${import.meta.env.VITE_BACKEND_API_URL}/auth/github`, an env-configured absolute URL. When that base is a different site from the app origin the click carries `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` and every login now 400s with raw JSON on the backend origin and no way back. The same applies to any cross-site entry point that 302s into `/auth/github` (Sec-Fetch-Site is downgraded to the most restrictive value across a redirect chain). The doc comment's justification ("SameSite=Lax already assumes frontend and backend share eTLD+1") is about session cookies, not about the OAuth state cookie, which is set and read purely on backend-origin top-level navigations and would work cross-site.

samples.summary: Pin-drop fallback fires on any NETWORK_ERROR, not just a proxy refusing CONNECT to an address literal
samples.evidence: The catch at lines 793-813 only checks `plan.pinnedThroughProxy` and `error.code === 'NETWORK_ERROR'`. A transient TCP reset, a TLS failure, or the origin simply being down on the first proxied hop therefore (a) permanently sets `pinThroughProxy = false` for the whole fetcher, (b) emits the alarming pin-dropped warning, and (c) silently retries the request by name. The retried request can then succeed against an address the gate never approved, and a genuine origin outage is reported as a pin problem. The comment claims "not attacker-triggerable", but an attacker-chosen host that simply refuses the first connection reaches the same state.

samples.summary: `rawRequest` throws an unclassified TypeError for null-body statuses (204/205/304)
samples.evidence: `new Response(Readable.toWeb(res.body), { status: res.statusCode })` (lines 677-680) throws `TypeError: Response with null body status cannot have body` whenever the origin answers 204, 205 or 304. This is the only path for pinned-proxy hops (`issue`, line 766) and the opaque-redirect fallback, so such a response crashes the export with a bare TypeError instead of the classified `httpError`/`SystemError` the rest of the module is careful to produce (exit 1, code `ERROR`).

samples.summary: `isOpaqueRedirect` also matches a network-error response, silently re-issuing the request on the real network and bypassing the injected `fetch`
samples.evidence: `isOpaqueRedirect` returns true for `res.status === 0` (line 635). A WHATWG *network error* response (`Response.error()`, type `'error'`, status 0) is indistinguishable here from an opaque redirect, so line 779-781 re-issues the hop through `undiciRequest`, ignoring the caller-supplied `opts.fetch`. A test seam or a runtime that returns a network-error response therefore has its failure converted into a real outbound request. The discarded first response's body is also never cancelled, unlike every other abandoned response in this loop (lines 824, 830).

samples.summary: Failure to bind the loopback callback port exits 1 (user error) although it is an environment fault, and prints the JSON envelope rather than login's prose
samples.evidence: `startCallbackServer` rejects with a plain `Error('Failed to start callback server')` (line 604) or the raw `ErrnoException` after 3 EADDRINUSE attempts (line 633). `classifyLoginFailure` returns `null` for both (it only recognises `LoginError`/`SystemError`/`UserError`), so the action rethrows, `runCli` catches it and `outputError` sets exit code 1. Under the new contract "the caller cannot fix a port-binding failure by retyping anything", so this should be the system class (2); it is also the one login failure that emits a JSON envelope instead of the prose the command otherwise promises.

samples.summary: `fetchLoginSession` parses JSON without a guard, so a non-JSON 2xx body escapes the exit contract as a raw SyntaxError
samples.evidence: `await exchangeRes.json()` (line 134), `await meRes.json()` (line 152) and `await wsRes.json()` (line 167) have no `.catch`. A 200 with an HTML body (a captive portal or a proxy error page — precisely the environments this PR added proxy handling for) throws a `SyntaxError`, which `classifyLoginFailure` returns `null` for, so the command dies with a stack trace instead of the documented one-line message. The rest of the CLI guards this (`HttpClient.sendJson`: `res.json().catch(() => null)`).

samples.summary: `exitCodeForStatus` classifies 429 (throttled) as a user error, so a rate-limited call exits 1 and agents will not retry
samples.evidence: `exitCodeForStatus` returns `EXIT_SYSTEM_ERROR` only for 401/403 and >=500. The backend throttles routes (`@Throttle` in packages/backend/src/api/v1/images.controller.ts and files.controller.ts, and `/auth/github/callback`), which yields 429. A 429 is transient and retryable — nothing the caller can fix by changing input — yet it now maps to exit 1 alongside 400/404, which is the class agents are told means "do not retry".

samples.summary: An empty or duplicated `Sec-Fetch-Site` header is treated as an attack
samples.evidence: `if (site === undefined) return;` only exempts a *missing* header. An empty-string value, or a duplicated header that Express joins into `'none, cross-site'`, falls through to `ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES.has(value)` → false → 400. The documented intent is that a client which does not meaningfully report the header is served; an empty value is the same situation.

finding.summary: Image gate hard-requires local DNS resolution, breaking exports on proxy-only / DNS-restricted machines — including images served by the configured API server
finding.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` unconditionally calls `await resolveHost(url, lookup, target)` (line 394) for every non-literal host, and `resolveHost` converts any lookup failure or empty answer into `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR')` (lines 267-279). verdict.reason: The cited code exists as described (image-fetcher.ts:394 always resolves non-literal hosts before planHop; resolveHost:264-280 turns lookup failure/empty answers into NETWORK_ERROR), but it is not a correctness defect. Fail-closed-on-unresolvable is the explicitly specified contract (docs/design/cli.md:1052-1057) and was mandated by a prior review that rejected the fail-open version ("a gate that fails open is not a gate", docs/tasks/active/20260803-cli-system-exit-code-lessons.md:64-71); the same spec states the gate is unchanged for proxied hops (cli.md:1074-1076), so resolving before planHop is required for the gate to have any verdict on a proxied request. The reviewer's secondary point is also factually wrong: the resolved addresses are the return value (:415) consumed as the connection pin (pinnedAgent at :526, proxied rewrite at :547-556 via :786-787), so the lookup is not redundant even when sameName is true. What remains is a security/availability tradeoff about DNS-restricted environments — owned by the security/design lens, not a wrong condition, inverted logic, missing guard, async mistake, or data-loss bug in the correctness lane.

verdict.reason: The guard code is present as quoted (github-auth.guard.ts:45,95,144-155 on GET /auth/github at auth.controller.ts:90-91), but the break it is claimed to cause requires a deployment where the frontend origin is cross-site from VITE_BACKEND_API_URL, and that configuration is already non-functional in this repo for reasons unrelated to the guard: browser auth is cookie-only with hardcoded sameSite:'lax' (auth.controller.ts:365-372; oauth-state.ts:142-157) and every frontend API call is a cross-origin fetch with credentials:"include" (packages/frontend/src/api/auth.ts:85-131,136-144), so a Lax cookie would never be sent and /auth/me would 401 forever; CORS is pinned to one FRONTEND_URL (main.ts:73-78). The actual deployments are same-site — wafflebase.io frontend vs https://api.wafflebase.io backend (frontend/.env.production:2, MAINTAINING.md:179) and dev localhost:5173 vs localhost:3000 (backend/README.md:21, frontend/README.md:29) — both of which the browser reports as Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site and the guard allows. For the redirect-chain half I enumerated every in-repo entry point into /auth/github: the frontend link (login-form.tsx:63), the CLI OS opener (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:262, yields 'none', allowed), and the confirmation page's relative same-origin href (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:138, page served from the backend origin at :110-113). No repo path 302s into /auth/github from another site. The refusal of genuinely cross-site-initiated logins is the documented intent (docs/design/backend.md:107, docs/design/rest-api.md:550).

finding.summary: `assertBrowserInitiated` refuses every `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` start, which breaks web login entirely on any deployment where the frontend and backend are not the same site
finding.evidence: `ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES = new Set(['none','same-origin','same-site'])` and anything else throws `BadRequestException`. The web login is a plain anchor navigation from the frontend (`packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:27`, `<Link to={VITE_BACKEND_API_URL}/auth/github>` — react-router treats a cross-origin absolute URL as an external link, so the browser navigates normally and sets `Sec-Fetch-Site` relative to the frontend origin). If the frontend is served from a different registrable domain or a different scheme than the backend (e.g. a CDN/preview host in front of `api.example.com`, or a dev setup with the frontend on `localhost:5173` and `VITE_BACKEND_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3000` — `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are not same-site), the header is `cross-site` and every login now 400s. Nothing in the config enforces same-site: CORS is keyed on `FRONTEND_URL` (docs/design/backend.md:604), which permits a cross-site frontend. The `SameSite=Lax` comment asserts the assumption but does not enforce it, and before this change a cross-site frontend still worked because no such check existed.

verdict.reason: The guard exists exactly as quoted (github-auth.guard.ts:45,144-155 refuse Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site with a 400), but the breakage it is said to cause cannot occur in any deployment this codebase supports, so it is not a blocking correctness defect. Counterexample: a cross-site frontend/backend deployment is already non-functional here regardless of the guard, because the session and refresh cookies are issued with sameSite: 'lax' (auth.controller.ts:365-372, whose own comment states "assumes frontend + backend share eTLD+1") while every authenticated frontend call is a non-navigational cross-origin fetch with credentials: "include" (frontend/src/api/auth.ts:35-38 /auth/refresh, :107-110 /auth/me, and the same pattern across src/api/*). Browsers withhold Lax cookies on such requests, so in the reviewer's scenarios (different registrable domain/scheme, or localhost:5173 frontend against 127.0.0.1:3000 backend) the user would land back logged out even before this check existed — the OAuth state cookies are Lax and __Host--prefixed for the same reason (oauth-state.ts:93-105,142-157). All documented configurations are same-site: self-hosting.md:27-28,43 and backend/README.md:21 pair localhost:5173 with localhost:3000 (same registrable domain; ports do not affect Sec-Fetch-Site, which reports same-site), and production pairs https://api.wafflebase.io (.env.production:2) with the wafflebase.io frontend. The behavior is also a deliberate, documented control with tests asserting it (docs/design/rest-api.md:550, docs/design/backend.md:107, github-auth.guard.spec.ts:190-221). No real login path yields cross-site, so there is no crash/broken-flow on a reachable path.

mergedFrom.summary: The CLI state entry is consumed before the browser-cookie check and before user creation, so any failure after that point (DB error in `findOrCreateUser`) burns the single-use state and forces a full `wafflebase login` restart

finding.summary: A CLI callback whose server-side state entry has expired is misclassified as a web flow and unconditionally clears the *web* state cookie, killing an unrelated in-flight web login in the same browser
finding.evidence: The flow is derived from `cliState?.mode === 'cli'`, where `cliState = this.cliAuthStore.consumeState(stateToken)`. `CliAuthStore` entries expire after 5 minutes (cli-auth.store.ts, `expiresAt: Date.now() + 5*60*1000`), and an in-memory store also misses on a different replica. When the entry is gone, a genuine CLI callback is treated as `'web'`, and `consumeOAuthState` then does `res.clearCookie(oauthStateCookieName('web'), ...)` (auth.controller.ts:269) *before* any validation — destroying the state cookie of a concurrent, unrelated web login the same browser has in flight, so that login later fails with 400 too. The CLI cookie meanwhile is never cleared. Any failed/replayed callback has the same side effect on the web cookie.

verdict.reason: The described code does not exist. (1) Flow selection is not derived from the store lookup: auth.controller.ts:150 branches on `isWebOAuthState(stateToken)`, a pure prefix test for 'web.' (oauth-state.ts:125-129), while CLI state tokens are base64url randomBytes (cli-auth.store.ts:60) and cannot carry that prefix — so an expired/absent CliAuthStore entry can never reclassify a CLI callback as web; it stays in the else-branch and ends at `throw new BadRequestException('CLI login state expired, invalid...')` (auth.controller.ts:218-221). The `state.mode === 'cli'` test at :185 is inside the already-chosen CLI branch. (2) There is no `consumeOAuthState` function anywhere in the repo, `oauthStateCookieName()` accepts no arguments (oauth-state.ts:49-51) so `oauthStateCookieName('web')` is not real code, and auth.controller.ts:269 is `const fromBody = ...` inside the unrelated refresh() handler. The only web-state clearCookie is at auth.controller.ts:160-163, lexically confined to the web branch and unreachable for a CLI state, so no concurrent web login's state cookie is destroyed. (3) The claim that the CLI cookie is never cleared is also false: it is cleared at auth.controller.ts:180-183 before consumeState at :184.
